results.result: Deep-sampling PCR (performing large numbers of replicate PCR reactions) extends the detection range of T. cruzi DNA in blood by at least three orders of magnitude compared to standard protocols. Using spiked blood samples, the method detected as few as 10^-7 parasite equivalents per reaction when sufficient replicates were performed, with all 40 aliquots at 10^-3 PE being positive and decreasing frequencies at lower concentrations.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C34 provide direct experimental evidence from Figure 1 showing dose-dependent detection across multiple orders of magnitude. The experimental design is sound with appropriate controls and quantification. Claim C4 accurately summarizes this finding as extending detection by at least three orders of magnitude.

results.result: DNA fragmentation increases PCR sensitivity by one order of magnitude, shifting the threshold for 100% positive reactions from 10^-3 to 10^-4 parasite equivalents per reaction. This improvement was demonstrated in both spiked samples and naturally infected macaque samples, with fragmented samples showing 80-100% positive reactions in 4 of 6 macaques using only 5 replicates.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C68 and C72 are directly supported by experimental data in Figures 4 and 4-supplements showing consistent improvement across multiple fragmentation methods and sample types. The mechanistic hypothesis (C62-C63) is reasonable and the quantitative improvement is well-documented.

results.result: Serial deep-sampling of fragmented DNA combined with multiple time points allowed detection of T. cruzi in all 21 seropositive macaques over a 12-month period, while all seronegative and previously cured macaques remained negative across >15,000 PCR reactions.
results.evaluation: Claims C44, C60-C61 provide strong evidence with appropriate positive and negative controls. The longitudinal sampling (C5, C25) demonstrates that temporal sampling is necessary for complete detection. The large number of negative reactions in controls establishes specificity.

results.result: Chronically infected individuals exhibit >6 log variation in stable parasite levels, ranging from animals with 9-10 of 10 reactions positive (likely detectable by standard PCR) to animals with <0.3% positive reactions across >3000 replicates. The frequency of positive PCR reactions strongly correlates with Cq values.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C47 provide quantitative data from Figure 2B and Figure 3 demonstrating the wide range. The statistical correlation (C47) is shown in Figure 3E. This represents a major finding about natural infection heterogeneity that was previously difficult to quantify.

results.result: The combination of DNA fragmentation and deep-sampling extends the quantifiable detection range to 10^-5 PE (using Cq values and percent positive) and remains linear to 10^-7 PE (using percent positive), representing ~2.4 × 10^-5 parasites/ml of blood or approximately single-copy DNA detection per reaction.
results.evaluation: Claims C73-C75 are directly supported by the dose-response data in Figure 5B showing linearity across the stated ranges. The calculation to parasites/ml and the inference about single-copy detection (C76) are reasonable given the known ~10^5 copies of satellite DNA per parasite.

results.result: A subset of recently infected macaques (2-4 years post-infection) with relatively high parasite burden exhibited a statistically significant (p<0.001) decline in parasite load over the 1-year study period, suggesting that immune control mechanisms can continue to drive parasite load lower during chronic infection.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C53 provide the observational data from Figure 3C with appropriate statistical analysis. The inference about immune mechanisms (C111) is reasonable though not directly tested. This represents a novel finding about infection dynamics in the chronic phase.

results.result: Parasite control can be rapidly lost when health status changes, as demonstrated by macaque P4 which switched from 100% PCR negative (384 reactions) to 50% positive coincident with development of severe gastrointestinal disease and pregnancy complications.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C59 provide detailed case data from Figure 3D with clinical and pathological information. This demonstrates that even well-controlled chronic infections can rapidly become uncontrolled, though this is a single case observation.

results.result: Parasite load is relatively stable over time in most chronically infected macaques, with no statistically significant correlation between length of infection and either frequency of positive PCR reactions (p=0.081) or mean Cq values (p=0.11).
results.evaluation: Claims C50, C55-C56 provide statistical analysis from Figure 3E showing lack of correlation with infection duration. Claim C109 appropriately contextualizes this finding with prior literature (Cerisola 1977). The stability is well-documented across the longitudinal data.

results.result: Hemoculture results correlated strongly with both the frequency of positive PCR reactions and average Cq values, with all macaques screened for ≥12 months being hemoculture positive in one or more samples (with one exception).
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C49 are supported by correlation data in Figure 3E-F. Hemoculture provides independent validation of the PCR results, though it is less sensitive and more labor-intensive than the deep-sampling PCR approach.

results.result: Frequent sampling (twice weekly for 4 weeks) showed similar irregular detection patterns as monthly sampling, with duplicate samples from the same needle stick sometimes showing dramatically different results. However, using fragmented DNA increased overall detection frequency >10-fold (2.2% to 27.5%) compared to non-fragmented samples.
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C71 are supported by data in Figure 5A demonstrating sampling variability and the benefit of fragmentation. Claim C96 provides a striking example of sampling error. This emphasizes the stochastic nature of detection at very low parasite levels.

results.result: The blood cell pellet is a more dependable source of T. cruzi DNA than plasma or whole blood, with plasma and whole blood showing all negative replicates in several cases when cell pellet DNA was majority positive.
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C79 are supported by comparative data in Figure 6. While plasma can be useful, the cell pellet provides more consistent detection. This is a practical finding for optimizing sample processing.

results.result: Humans and dogs exhibit a similar broad range of T. cruzi burdens as macaques, reinforcing the appropriateness of dogs and non-human primates as models of human infection.
results.evaluation: Claim C80 is directly supported by data in Figure 7 showing comparable ranges across species. Claim C128 appropriately interprets this as validation of animal models. The sample size for humans is limited (n=9) but shows the expected range.

results.result: Animals with detectable blood parasite DNA also had PCR-amplifiable DNA in multiple tissue samples.
results.evaluation: Claim C81 is supported by data in Figure 7-supplement 1. This confirms that blood detection correlates with tissue infection, though the number of animals examined is limited (n=3).

results.result: Deep-sampling PCR monitoring of benznidazole treatment in three dogs revealed variable treatment responses, with one dog requiring increased dosing frequency (from 2× to 3× weekly) to achieve undetectable parasite levels, demonstrating that treatment monitoring allows dosing adjustments for improved outcomes.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C85 are supported by treatment monitoring data in Figure 8. This demonstrates the practical utility of the method for treatment monitoring, though proof of cure requires longer follow-up after treatment cessation.

results.result: Deep-sampling PCR offers the first true test of cure for Chagas disease and should fulfill the need for an assay that detects treatment success rather than only failure.
results.evaluation: Claims C29 and C117 make strong assertions about providing a "test of cure," but this requires demonstration that sustained negative results after treatment truly indicate sterile cure rather than just very low parasite levels below detection. The method's sensitivity is well-established, but validation as a definitive test of cure requires longer-term follow-up data and comparison with treatment failures.

results.result: Deep-sampling PCR should assist in determining associations between parasite load, immune parameters, and disease risk, and even subjects with very low parasite burden should be considered for treatment. Selection of subjects with higher pre-treatment parasite loads for clinical trials would facilitate detection of treatment failures.
results.evaluation: Claims C30 and C121 are reasonable recommendations based on the method's capabilities, but represent future applications rather than demonstrated results. Claim C113 is a clinical recommendation based on the P4 case, but this is extrapolated from a single observation.

results.result: Detection of T. cruzi DNA in infected hosts is primarily a problem of subsampling error at two levels: blood samples represent only ~0.2% of total blood volume, and PCR aliquots represent 1/100th to 1/250th of recovered DNA. When parasite numbers are very low, detection becomes essentially random.
results.evaluation: Claims C93-C98 provide a clear mechanistic explanation for detection variability, supported by the experimental observations (particularly C96 from Figure 5) and cited literature (C94). This represents an important conceptual framework for understanding the method's necessity.

results.result: DNA fragmentation reduces subsampling error by dispersing target sequences more evenly throughout the blood DNA sample, leading to increased frequency and consistency of positive PCR reactions. Fragmentation should be incorporated as a standard step even when deep-sampling is not used, though the ultimate limiting factor remains the total blood volume collected.
results.evaluation: Claims C100-C101 provide a mechanistic explanation supported by the experimental data in Figures 4-5. The recommendation (C103) is justified by the demonstrated benefits. Claim C104 correctly identifies the fundamental limitation of the approach.

results.result: Deep-sampling PCR does not require special equipment but necessitates extreme care in sample preparation and will be expensive, time-consuming, and labor-intensive, requiring hundreds of PCR reactions on DNA from 10+ high-volume blood samples per subject.
results.evaluation: Claims C118-C119 accurately describe the practical requirements and limitations of the method. The contamination prevention protocols described in Materials and Methods support the need for extreme care. This is an honest assessment of the method's feasibility.

results.result: Future improvements may include multiplexing additional PCR targets, optimizing DNA fragmentation further, or using new technologies like UltraPCR to reduce the number of replicate reactions needed, potentially making PCR-based detection of all T. cruzi-infected subjects routine.
results.evaluation: Claims C122-C125 are speculative about future improvements and cite relevant technologies, but do not present experimental validation of these approaches. These represent reasonable directions for future work rather than demonstrated results.

results.result: The authors claim that DNA fragmentation combined with deep-sampling PCR extends the quantitative detection range of T. cruzi by at least three orders of magnitude (claims C4, C75), with fragmentation alone shifting the 100% positive threshold from 10^-3 to 10^-4 PE/reaction (C64, C72), and deep-sampling enabling detection down to 10^-7 PE/reaction (C34, C74). These findings are based on spiked blood sample experiments shown in Figures 1, 4A, and 5B.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 raises significant methodological concerns about the detection and quantification limits, noting inconsistencies between theoretical expectations and observed results. Specifically, the reviewer questions the high amplification rates at 10^-7 PE (30% positive when ~1% would be expected) and at 10^-6 PE (40% positive when much lower rates would be expected based on target copy calculations). The reviewer suggests these discrepancies may indicate 'inaccurate quantification of the starting number of parasites' or 'random contamination,' and calculates that some observed results are 'highly improbable' (probability ~1 in 100,000). While reviewers 1 and 2 acknowledge the method shows promise in 'expanding detection limits,' the editor notes 'some variability in the limits of detection,' indicating uncertainty about the precise sensitivity claims.

results.result: The authors claim that deep sampling of fragmented DNA combined with serial blood sampling enabled detection of T. cruzi in all 21 seropositive macaques over a 12-month period (C44), including extremely difficult cases with only 0.21-0.29% positive reactions (C45), and that this approach can confirm even the most difficult to detect infections (C25).
results.evaluation: Reviewers 1 and 2 both affirm this finding. Reviewer 1 states the methods 'enabled consistent detection of the parasite in infected humans, non-human primates, and dogs, including hosts with very low parasitemia levels.' The editor confirms 'the evidence is sound for macaques' and notes the findings 'offer solid evidence of enhanced detection sensitivity.' No reviewer challenges the claim that all seropositive macaques were eventually detected.

results.result: The authors report a >6 log variation in stable parasite levels between chronically infected individuals (C6, C26), supported by a strong negative correlation between PCR positivity frequency and Cq values (C47), demonstrating that individuals control infections to vastly different degrees (C108).
results.evaluation: The editor explicitly states the findings 'shed light on parasite load dynamics during chronic infection' and reviewers do not challenge the wide range of parasite loads observed. Reviewer 1 notes the study 'captured parasitemia dynamics' effectively. The correlation data in Figure 3E supporting this finding is not questioned by any reviewer.

results.result: The authors report that three recently infected macaques (2-4 years post-infection) with relatively high parasite burdens showed a statistically significant (p<0.001) decline in parasite load over the 1-year study period (C52, C110), suggesting immune control mechanisms can drive parasite load lower during chronic infection (C111).
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge this finding. Reviewer 1 acknowledges the study provides 'valuable insights' into 'parasitemia dynamics' and the editor confirms the findings 'shed light on parasite load dynamics during chronic infection.' The statistical significance and longitudinal data in Figure 3C are not questioned.

results.result: The authors report that macaque P4 showed a dramatic increase in parasite load when health status changed (pregnancy complications leading to euthanasia), demonstrating that parasite control can be quickly lost when health/immune status changes (C8, C28, C112).
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge this case study. Reviewer 1 notes the work 'stresses the importance of treating individuals with low parasitic loads, as immune control may change over time,' which aligns with this finding. The clinical and pathological data for P4 are not questioned.

results.result: The authors propose that DNA fragmentation reduces subsampling error by breaking linked target sequences into smaller fragments that are more evenly distributed (C62, C63, C100), and demonstrate experimentally that fragmentation increases PCR sensitivity by one order of magnitude (C64, C102) and improves detection consistency in both spiked samples and naturally infected macaque samples (C66, C67, C68).
results.evaluation: While reviewers 1 and 2 acknowledge fragmentation as a methodological innovation, reviewer 3 identifies inconsistencies between fragmented and non-fragmented results. The reviewer notes that 'Figure 4A (not fragmented) shows lower values of positivity than Figure 1 for 10^-5 and 10^-6 dilutions showing this inconsistency among experiments,' suggesting either quantification errors or contamination issues. Reviewer 2 notes that 'the reliance on blood cell pellets and the DNA fragmentation protocol introduces extra processing steps' that may limit practical adoption, but does not challenge the technical effectiveness.

results.result: The authors demonstrate substantial sampling variability, showing that duplicate blood samples collected simultaneously can yield dramatically different PCR results (C70, C96), and that fragmented DNA from year 2 samples showed >10-fold higher positivity rates than non-fragmented year 1 samples (C71).
results.evaluation: Reviewers acknowledge the sampling variability findings. Reviewer 1 states 'Serial testing across multiple blood samples mitigated the variability in parasitemia, addressing challenges first noted in early xenodiagnosis studies.' The demonstration of subsampling error is not challenged and supports the rationale for the deep-sampling approach.

results.result: The authors report that blood cell pellets are a more dependable source for T. cruzi DNA detection than plasma or whole blood, as plasma and whole blood had all negative replicates in several cases when cell pellet replicates were majority positive (C78, C79).
results.evaluation: Reviewer 1 explicitly notes 'the findings suggest that cell pellets from blood yield higher concentrations of parasite DNA compared to whole blood, prompting a reevaluation of current diagnostic practices, which predominantly use whole blood lysates.' The editor's summary mentions 'blood cell pellet analysis' as part of the methodological advance. This finding is not challenged.

results.result: The authors demonstrate that humans and dogs exhibit a similar range of T. cruzi burdens as macaques (C80), supporting the appropriateness of dogs and NHPs as models of human infection (C128), as shown in Figure 7.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 raises concerns about the human sample data, noting that 'Of the 9 samples tested, 6 (56%) were consistently amplified in all or nearly all reactions, indicating these samples could also be reliably detected with standard PCR protocols. Two additional samples were detected only with the deep-sampling approach, increasing sensitivity to 78%; however, these detections might be attributable to random chance given the limited sample size.' The editor acknowledges 'small sample size of human samples' as a limitation. While the method works in humans, the incremental benefit over standard PCR and the comparability to macaques remain uncertain.

results.result: The authors claim that deep-sampling PCR offers the first true test of cure for Chagas disease (C29, C117) and demonstrate its utility in treatment monitoring through three dogs with different benznidazole treatment outcomes (C82, C83), showing that rigorous assessment allows dosing adjustments for higher treatment success (C85).
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 questions the 'unclear relevance for treatment monitoring in Humans,' noting that the improvement over conventional PCR in human samples is modest and may be due to chance given the small sample size. Reviewer 2 acknowledges the method's 'potential for enhancing treatment monitoring' but emphasizes that 'broader adoption depends on the development of cost-effective and scalable alternatives to labor-intensive techniques.' The dog treatment data are not directly challenged, but the claim of being a 'test of cure' for humans is not fully supported by the evidence presented.

results.result: The authors report that seronegative controls and cured macaques were PCR and hemoculture negative in >15,000 collective PCR reactions (C43, C60, C61), demonstrating assay specificity.
results.evaluation: While the negative control data are presented, reviewer 3 raises critical concerns about contamination detection: 'the manuscript does not provide enough details on how cross-contamination was detected or managed. It is unclear how the negative controls (NTCs) and no-template controls were distributed across plates, in terms of both quantity and placement.' The reviewer emphasizes this is 'critical, as the low detection thresholds targeted in this study increase the risk of false positives by contamination.' Without adequate contamination control documentation, the specificity claims remain uncertain.

results.result: The authors acknowledge that deep-sampling PCR does not require special equipment but is expensive, time-consuming, and labor-intensive (C118, C119).
results.evaluation: Reviewer 2 explicitly states this as a weakness: 'the reliance on blood cell pellets and the DNA fragmentation protocol introduces extra processing steps, which may not be feasible for many clinical laboratories, particularly in resource-limited endemic areas that require simpler and more streamlined procedures.' Reviewer 2 also notes 'broader adoption depends on the development of cost-effective and scalable alternatives to labor-intensive techniques such as sonication.' The practical limitations are acknowledged by reviewers.

comparisons.comparison: Both address detection limits and sensitivity claims (C4, C32-C34, C64, C72-C75, C102). OpenEval finds the evidence SUPPORTED with sound experimental design. Peer review rates UNCERTAIN due to Reviewer 3's methodological concerns about inconsistencies between theoretical and observed amplification rates, potential contamination, and quantification accuracy issues at extreme dilutions.

Both evaluate consistent parasite detection in chronically infected hosts (C5, C25, C44). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED with strong controls and longitudinal evidence. Peer review also rates SUPPORTED, with reviewers affirming detection in all seropositive macaques and acknowledging solid evidence of enhanced sensitivity.

Both address wide range of parasite loads during chronic infection (C6, C26, C47, C108). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED as a major finding about infection heterogeneity. Peer review also rates SUPPORTED, with editor and reviewers acknowledging insights into parasite load dynamics without challenging the correlation data.

Both evaluate fluctuating parasitemia patterns (C7, C27, C51-C53, C110-C111). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED as a novel finding about chronic phase dynamics, noting the immune mechanism inference is reasonable though not directly tested. Peer review also rates SUPPORTED, acknowledging valuable insights into parasitemia dynamics without challenging the statistical significance.

Both address the P4 case of rapid parasite load increase (C8, C28, C57-C59, C112). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED but notes it's a single case observation. Peer review also rates SUPPORTED, with reviewers acknowledging the importance of treating low parasitic loads as immune control may change over time.

Both evaluate DNA fragmentation benefits (C62-C68, C100-C103). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED with consistent improvement across multiple methods and sample types. Peer review rates UNCERTAIN due to Reviewer 3's identification of inconsistencies between fragmented and non-fragmented results, suggesting possible quantification errors or contamination, though technical effectiveness is acknowledged.

Both address sampling variability and subsampling error (C69-C71, C96). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED, emphasizing stochastic detection at low parasite levels. Peer review also rates SUPPORTED, with reviewers acknowledging serial testing mitigates variability and the demonstration supports the deep-sampling rationale.

Both evaluate cell pellet versus plasma comparison (C78-C79). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED as a practical finding for sample processing optimization. Peer review also rates SUPPORTED, with Reviewer 1 explicitly noting cell pellets yield higher parasite DNA concentrations and prompting reevaluation of diagnostic practices.

Both address comparable parasite ranges across species (C80, C128). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED as validation of animal models, noting limited human sample size (n=9). Peer review rates UNCERTAIN due to Reviewer 3's concerns about human sample data, noting most could be detected with standard PCR and questioning incremental benefit given small sample size.

Both evaluate treatment monitoring utility (C82-C85, with R10 also covering C29, C117). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED for demonstrating practical utility in dogs, noting longer follow-up needed for proof of cure. Peer review rates UNCERTAIN, questioning relevance for human treatment monitoring due to modest improvement over conventional PCR and small sample size.

OpenEval R3 addresses specificity with controls (C60-C61) and finds SUPPORTED. Peer R11 evaluates similar specificity claims (C43, C60-C61) but rates UNCERTAIN due to Reviewer 3's concerns about inadequate contamination control documentation and lack of details on negative control distribution across plates.

Both address practical limitations and feasibility (C118-C119). OpenEval finds SUPPORTED as an honest assessment of method requirements. Peer review also rates SUPPORTED, with Reviewer 2 explicitly noting extra processing steps may not be feasible for resource-limited settings and broader adoption depends on cost-effective alternatives.

OpenEval R5 evaluates dose-response linearity and single-copy detection inference (C73-C76). Peer R1 partially overlaps (C73-C75) but focuses on detection limit concerns. OpenEval finds SUPPORTED; peer review rates the broader detection claims UNCERTAIN due to methodological inconsistencies at extreme dilutions.

OpenEval R15 evaluates 'test of cure' claims (C29, C116-C117) and rates UNCERTAIN, requiring longer follow-up validation. Peer R10 also addresses test of cure (C29, C117) and rates UNCERTAIN, questioning human relevance and noting modest improvement over conventional PCR may be due to chance.

OpenEval R8 addresses stability of parasite loads over infection duration and lack of correlation with duration (C50, C55-C56, C109). No corresponding peer review evaluation found addressing these specific claims about temporal stability.
